acquisition.why: Getting subscribers is inbound and legal through Meta lead ads, Beehiiv Boosts and referrals, and agents can run it. Getting sponsors is the revenue side. It is mostly manual relationship selling to local businesses, many of them sole traders who cannot be cold-emailed. An inbound 'advertise with us' page and selling to business-owner subscribers help, but a human is still needed to close [E].

onboarding.why: Beehiiv automates subscriber welcome emails and surveys. Sponsor onboarding (brief, artwork, scheduling) can be templated with an agent and a form.

delivery.why: Agents can scrape events and council or venue sources and draft the weekly email. Local accuracy still needs a human check of about 30-60 minutes a week; the Winnipeg operator still does a nightly review.

billing.why: Stripe invoices or payment links for sponsor slots. Beehiiv handles any paid tier.

support.why: Reader replies are low volume and agents can triage them. Sponsor queries and complaints need occasional human answers.

scores.R_why: Ricardo lives in Bromley, which gives a genuine local-knowledge edge, and the content is AI-assisted, so it fits 6-8 hours a week. £300 of Meta ads at a likely UK cost of £0.80-1.50 per lead buys about 200-350 subscribers [E]. That is enough to test engagement but well below the 2-5k list needed before sponsors pay [E]. Sponsor sales take a human's time and will be slow. Consent capture and the privacy policy must be done properly under UK GDPR.
scores.M_why: Local news deserts are real and local newsletters are growing in the UK. The risks are London borough coverage by existing local titles and community Facebook groups, plus rising Meta cost per lead. A local audience with first-party data is harder for AI to commoditise than generic content.
scores.one_line: Good fit for Bromley: agent-written content and inbound subscriber growth are legal and cheap. The bottleneck is human sponsor sales, so revenue lags by many months [E].

acquisition.why: Paid social, Beehiiv Boosts and recommendations, and SEO-indexed archives are inbound and agents can run them. Spend must be optimised so cost per subscriber stays below revenue per subscriber. Direct sponsor outreach can legally go by cold email to limited companies.

onboarding.why: Signup, welcome sequence and lead magnets are fully automated in Beehiiv.

delivery.why: Agents can research and draft. A niche newsletter's value depends on voice, insight and accuracy, so a human edits each issue.

billing.why: Beehiiv's ad network and Boosts pay automatically. Direct sponsor slots are invoiced through Stripe.

support.why: Low support load: unsubscribes are automated and agents can handle sponsor scheduling.

scores.R_why: Cheap to start and fits the hours. £300 buys only about 150-300 paid subscribers [E], and meaningful sponsor income usually needs 5-10k engaged readers, so expect 12+ months to reach real revenue [E]. Earning by sending Boosts to other newsletters is possible, but the yield is small.
scores.M_why: Saturated: AI-written newsletters are flooding inboxes, open rates are falling, and sponsors concentrate on the top titles. A defensible niche needs domain expertise, which Ricardo has in tech, but that niche is crowded too.
scores.one_line: Low-cost, mostly automatable media asset. Sources lean on survivors (The Hustle, Sahil Bloom), and the route to sponsor revenue is slow and crowded for a part-timer [E].

acquisition.why: Inbound SEO and app directories are legal, but 'AI business plan generator' keywords are dominated by established players. The sources relied on existing audiences, which Ricardo does not have.

onboarding.why: A web form, with no human involved.

delivery.why: Prompt pipeline plus LLM produces the output unattended.

support.why: Refund requests and quality complaints can be handled by an agent under a refund policy.

scores.R_why: Trivial for Ricardo to build in a weekend and it fits the hours and budget. The weak point is demand: ChatGPT and Claude give the same output free or within subscriptions users already pay for. Content needs a disclaimer that it is not financial or legal advice.
scores.M_why: Heavily commoditised: dozens of free generators exist alongside LivePlan and Upmetrics AI, and general-purpose LLMs are direct substitutes. Little willingness to pay a one-off £15-20 [E].
scores.one_line: Fully automatable but close to worthless as a business: there is no revenue evidence, only a '45-minute build' demo, and free LLMs substitute for it directly.

acquisition.why: YouTube's algorithm serves dubbed audio tracks to foreign viewers, which is inbound. This only works on top of an existing large channel.

onboarding.why: Not applicable: it is your own content, with no customers to onboard.

delivery.why: The dubbing pipeline and upload can be automated. Spot-checking translation quality is light.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has no YouTube channel with large view counts. Building one to the point where dubbing adds meaningful revenue takes years and on-camera effort, which is unrealistic at 6-8 hours a week. Pivoting to dubbing other creators' videos as a service would be a different, sales-led business.
scores.M_why: YouTube's native auto-dubbing is rolling out widely, so it commoditises the edge. Foreign-language RPMs, Spanish and Arabic for example, are often well below the claimed $8 [E].
scores.one_line: A good add-on for creators who already have large audiences, but not a standalone business for Ricardo, and YouTube's native dubbing erodes it.

acquisition.why: Developer SEO, answer-engine (LLM) pickup, build-in-public posts on X and Google Ads are all inbound. Agents can produce problem-led docs and articles.

delivery.why: Unattended software, but platform API changes (Meta, X, TikTok, LinkedIn) break integrations and app reviews need human attention.

support.why: The source ran human live chat around the clock. Agents with good docs can handle most of it, but integration debugging escalates to Ricardo.

scores.R_why: Matches Ricardo's technical skills. The burdens are platform app approvals, X API tier costs (often well above £100 a month [E]), OAuth token security under UK GDPR, and constant API breakage. That maintenance is heavy for 6-8 hours a week and a £300 budget.
scores.M_why: Crowded: Ayrshare, Post Bridge, Upload-Post, late.dev and Buffer already compete. A $10 entry price and 17%+ churn mean a race to the bottom, and platform terms can cut off access.
scores.one_line: An agent-friendly developer SaaS with credible first-hand MRR, but only one source. It sits in a crowded, platform-dependent niche where maintenance would eat Ricardo's limited hours.

acquisition.why: SEO free tools and templates are inbound and agents can run them. 'E-signature' SERPs are entrenched, and the incumbent's success relied on an aged domain and years of content. Early cold email would need to target limited companies only.

support.why: Signing failures and legal-validity questions arise. Agents can answer most, with escalations to Ricardo.

scores.R_why: Easy to build, but buyers expect audit trails, security and SOC 2 or ISO credibility. SEO takes 12-24+ months to pay off, so £300 and 6-8 hours a week will not get traction against established domains [E].
scores.M_why: Commoditised: DocuSign, Adobe, Dropbox Sign, Zoho, PandaDoc and many free tools compete. E-signing is also bundled into Google Workspace and Microsoft products.
scores.one_line: Ideal automation profile, but in a saturated, trust-heavy category where the incumbent's SEO moat is the whole business. Low headroom for a newcomer.

acquisition.why: Cold email to e-commerce brands that are limited companies is legal, and agents can build Meta Ads Library prospect lists and free sample ads. Closing $2-5k retainers needs human sales calls. LinkedIn DMs to individuals are risky under the PECR rules given.

onboarding.why: Brand briefs and asset intake can be templated. Each client needs a kickoff and alignment on tone and claims.

delivery.why: Generation pipelines (Arcads/Higgsfield via n8n) do most of the work. Curation, brand fit and ASA/CAP compliance checks need human review, especially for supplement health claims.

support.why: Revision requests, performance complaints and churn conversations are human-heavy.

scores.R_why: A retainer agency needs responsiveness, sales calls and revisions, which are hard at 6-8 hours a week with a toddler. Tool subscriptions (around $1k for Arcads) exceed the £300 budget. Under ASA/CAP and DMCC fake-review rules, AI testimonials are a legal risk in the UK.
scores.M_why: Commoditising fast: brands can use Arcads or Higgsfield themselves, many copycat agencies exist, and Meta keeps adding native generative AI creative tools.
scores.one_line: Real demand, but this is a service agency with human sales and revisions. Its evidence comes largely from tool tutorials with affiliate links and hypothetical funnel maths, and the market is commoditising.

acquisition.why: Google and Meta ads and SEO are legal inbound channels, but untested in the sources. UK trades are mostly sole traders, so cold email, SMS or DMs are barred, and outreach in Facebook groups needs a human.

onboarding.why: Self-serve signup is possible. Non-technical trades users often need data import and hand-holding.

delivery.why: Hosted SaaS runs unattended. AI-generated code needs ongoing maintenance and security work.

support.why: Operational software for small businesses creates urgent, human-heavy support around bookings and payments.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it. Handling client and customer data under UK GDPR, taking payments and deposits, and supporting businesses that depend on it is a lot for 6-8 hours a week. £300 of ads only tests one niche [E]. The niche should suit the UK, for example tattoo studios or dog groomers rather than pool services.
scores.M_why: UK trade CRMs (Tradify, Jobber, ServiceM8, Fergus, Powered Now) and niche booking tools already exist, and AI makes clones cheap. There is some headroom in micro-niches, but switching costs and low willingness to pay are real.
scores.one_line: Technically feasible and billing is easy to automate, but the sources are build demos with zero customers. Legal acquisition for sole-trader trades is hard and support load is high.
